chunks.text: Sal (Shorea robusta), also called shala, sakhua or sarai, belongs to the Dipterocarpaceae family (order Malvales) and was formally described by C. F. Gaertner. It is native to the Indian subcontinent, forming vast forests across a belt running from Chhattisgarh, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha and Jharkhand westward to the Shivalik Hills, and through the Eastern Ghats and the Vindhya-Satpura ranges of central India; it also occurs in Bangladesh, Nepal, Tibet and Myanmar. Mature trees reach up to 40 m in height with trunk diameters up to 2 m, and bear broad, leathery leaves 10-25 cm long and 5-15 cm wide. In wetter areas sal stays evergreen, while in drier tracts it is deciduous, shedding leaves from February to April and flushing new foliage in April-May. Fossil evidence from lignite deposits in Rajasthan and Gujarat shows that sal or closely related Shorea species have dominated forests on the Indian subcontinent since at least the early Eocene, around 49 million years ago — remarkable evolutionary continuity. The species is currently assessed as Near Threatened by the IUCN, and is the official state tree of both Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

Sal is one of India's most important sources of hardwood timber — the wood is hard, coarse-grained, resinous and very durable, though difficult to plane and polish, and has traditionally been used for door and window frames and heavy construction (historically including railway sleepers). Dried sal leaves are stitched together into patravali, biodegradable disposable plates and bowls widely used in eastern and central India, which livestock will eat once discarded. The tree also yields sal dammar (Indian dammar), a resin used as incense in Hindu ritual, as an astringent in Ayurvedic preparations, and even for marine caulking; its seed oil, once refined, has been used both as a cooking oil and as lamp oil.

Sal carries deep religious significance in both Hinduism and Buddhism. In Hindu tradition it is associated with Vishnu, and its name derives from the Sanskrit 'shala' meaning 'rampart'; the temple sculpture motif of the salabhanjika — a yakshini grasping a flowering sal branch — became a recurring feature of classical Indian temple architecture. In Buddhist tradition, Queen Maya is said to have given birth to the Buddha at Lumbini while holding the branch of a sal tree, and the Buddha is said to have passed away (attained parinirvana) lying between a pair of sal trees — the tree's brief flowering period is used in Buddhist teaching as a symbol of impermanence.
